title: Camp 4 close
hook: the whole strand, all 21 Camp 1 words, the Gita done
tomorrow: Isha Upanishad (18 verses, one week): "all this is pervaded by the Lord" (1 of 7)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Gita in the world. Thoreau at the pond, Tilak in a cell, Vivekananda, Gandhi. Your line was who else carried it. Did someone tell you what carried them? Today, the last day of the camp. Day two hundred thirty-one.
screen: `GITA IN THE WORLD — WHO ELSE CARRIED IT.`

segments.voice: In ancient India, a student lived for years in the teacher's house, learning the Vedas by heart. When the studies were done, there was a ceremony called samavartana: the return home. The student bathed, put on new clothes, and the teacher gave a last talk. One version of that talk survives in the Taittiriya Upanishad. Speak the truth. Practice dharma. Don't neglect your study. Treat your mother, your father, your teacher and your guest as the divine. Then the student walked home, carrying it all. Today is your samavartana.
screen: `YEARS IN THE TEACHER'S HOUSE.` → `SPEAK THE TRUTH. PRACTICE DHARMA.` → `THEN, THE WALK HOME.`

segments.voice: Look at what you're carrying. It started with twenty-one words, back in camp one. Namaste. Om. Dharma. Shanti. Pranam. Ganesha. Mantra. Puja. Karma. Atman. Brahman. Guru. Japa. Arti. Seva. Bhakti. Ahimsa. Maya. Moksha. Satsang. And the twenty-first, the Gita itself, the mountain ahead, with its line: you have the right to act, not to the fruit. Then the stories, then the practices. And then, for seventy-five days, the text itself, a few verses at a time. Chapter one, a man collapsing in a chariot. Chapter eighteen, the same man standing up and saying, my confusion is gone. This last week drew it together. The last instruction: do not grieve. Sanjaya's closing: wherever Krishna and Arjuna are, there is victory. The whole book in one session. Your twelve verses, chosen by you. One verse a day, going forward. And the people who carried it before you. Here's what's worth saying plainly. Plenty of people keep a Gita on the shelf and never read it through. You have. Not in a weekend, not by skimming, but slowly, one piece of the conversation at a time. That counts. Tomorrow the path goes deeper. Camp five is the depths: the Upanishads, the texts the Gita itself draws on. We start with the Isha Upanishad, eighteen verses in a week, and its first line: all this is pervaded by the Lord. But today, just take the bath, put on the new clothes, and walk home carrying it. That's the word today: graduation.
screen: `TWENTY-ONE WORDS.` · `SEVENTY-FIVE DAYS OF THE TEXT.` · `YOU READ IT THROUGH.` · `NEXT: THE DEPTHS.` · then, large: `GRADUATION.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the camp one words pass through you once more, slowly, one breath each if you like. Namaste. Om. Dharma. Shanti. Let them come in any order. Then let the Gita come as a single picture: the chariot, the two, the dawn over the field. Then bring to mind your one verse for today. Hold it. You don't have to do anything with it. Just notice that it's yours now. The bell holds the time.
Graduation. In the old tradition, samavartana, the student's return home, with a last teaching: speak the truth, practice dharma, don't neglect your study.
Your line: you actually read it. Today, let yourself feel that, just once, without rushing past it. Tomorrow, the depths. Day two hundred thirty-one.

howItsDone: In traditional Hindu education, the end of study was marked by samavartana, the student's ceremonial return home, and the teacher's final advice in Taittiriya Upanishad 1.11 is still recited at some convocations in India; many Hindus mark finishing the Gita with a full recitation or a small puja.

fork.setup: you're a student finishing years in the teacher's house. the studies are done. what happens next?
options: samavartana: a bath, new clothes, a last teaching, and the walk home.
fork.reveal: samavartana, the return. the Taittiriya Upanishad preserves a teacher's last words to the student.

original.note: Sanskrit: samavartana, returning home: the rite marking the end of a student's years of Vedic study.

trapdoor: what you thought: graduation is a ceremony and a certificate.
what it means: in the old tradition it's a return home, carrying what you learned into ordinary life.

what a scholar hears: samavartana is one of the Hindu samskaras; Taittiriya Upanishad 1.11 ('satyam vada, dharmam chara, svadhyayan ma pramadah') is traditionally read as the teacher's convocation address.
